_comment: The kind of speaking occasion a report covers, keyed by speech_id.
Drives the index grouping and -- the reason this file exists -- the
partition for every rate statistic on the site.
AUTHORED, NEVER DERIVED. The tempting heuristic is 'a President gave
it, so it is a presidential address'; that is wrong for a candidate
debate, a press conference, and a Senate floor speech given by a
former President. Class is a property of the OCCASION, not of the
speaker's office, so each entry is a judgement recorded by hand.
WHY IT GATES STATISTICS. A State of the Union and a Senate floor
speech are not the same genre: different length, different rhetorical
register, different density of checkable claims. Pooling them into one
rate would let a floor speech's score be read against a SOTU baseline,
which the corpus cannot support. Rates are computed WITHIN a class and
never across classes.
NO RESERVED CLASSES. This file is the whole authority on what classes
exist; the renderer does not carry a hardcoded allowlist. A speech_id
with no entry here is 'unclassified': it still renders and stays
visible, but is excluded from every rate statistic. Failing closed
that way means forgetting to classify a new report understates the
corpus rather than silently contaminating another class's numbers.
'order' fixes the index section order. It is authored too -- there is
no meaningful sort key over class names, and alphabetical order would
put a new class somewhere arbitrary.
'labels_inline' is the mid-sentence form ('the five presidential
addresses checked'). It is authored rather than lower-cased from
'labels' because casing is not mechanical: 'Presidential addresses'
de-capitalises mid-sentence but 'Senate' is a proper noun and does
not. Deriving it would silently produce 'the four senate floor
speeches checked'.
